**Priority: MEDIUM**

newsletters.subject: Extra usage for Ollama’s Pro and Max plans
newsletters.summary:
## Ollama Newsletter

**Priority: MEDIUM**

### Top Updates
- Ollama has introduced extra usage for its Pro and Max plans, allowing users to purchase additional usage when they reach their 5-hour session or weekly usage limit, ensuring uninterrupted access to the platform without waiting for the limit to reset. This is particularly useful for users who need more flexible and continuous access to Ollama's large language models.
- The extra usage can be managed in the settings section of the Ollama website, and users can also enable automatic reloading to refresh their extra usage balance without interruption. Additionally, spend limits can be set to control how much extra usage will be automatically reloaded for a given month.
- Ollama's extra usage consumes credits 4-6x more efficiently than usage credits for proprietary models, making it a cost-effective option for users. Furthermore, extra usage credits can be used towards all models on Ollama's cloud, including GLM-5.2, which is hosted in the US with zero data retention.
- For users not yet on a Pro or Max plan, Ollama offers the option to upgrade their plan to access larger models using Ollama's cloud, highlighting the platform's focus on efficient pricing and open models.
- The newsletter also touches on the broader context of Ollama's developments, including the release of Ollama v0.8, which adds streaming responses and tool calling, allowing local models to invoke external tools and real-time web search. This feature effectively turns a local LLM into a more agent-like assistant.
- Ollama has also unveiled a new multimodal AI engine, separate from the original llama.cpp base, implemented in Go with optimizations such as KV-cache and image caching, chunked attention, and 2D rotary embeddings. This significantly improves local reasoning performance and large-image handling.
- The security and operational concerns surrounding Ollama infrastructure have been highlighted, with researchers identifying over 175,000 publicly exposed Ollama servers and critical vulnerabilities. This emphasizes the need for proper hardening and monitoring of Ollama infrastructure, treating it as high-value, internet-facing compute.

### Notable Links
- [Ollama Settings](https://ollama.com/settings)
- [Add Extra Usage](https://ollama.com/extra-usage)
- [Upgrade Your Plan](https://ollama.com/pricing)

additionalContext.context:
Anthropic is an AI research company founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers, best known for its Claude family of large language models, which compete directly with OpenAI’s GPT series and Google’s Gemini models.[2] It focuses on building advanced, generally capable AI systems with an emphasis on safety, alignment, and enterprise use cases, and has become one of the key “foundation model” labs shaping the current AI landscape.[2] This matters because Anthropic’s models are increasingly embedded in developer platforms and cloud ecosystems, influencing how AI is integrated into products across legal, sales, marketing, data analysis, and software engineering workflows.[1][6]  

Recent developments show Anthropic both pushing model capabilities and rapidly scaling its infrastructure. The company has released **Claude Opus 4.7**, its latest flagship model, making it generally available through its own API and major cloud platforms such as Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud’s Vertex AI, and Microsoft’s Foundry, while keeping premium pricing aimed at high‑value enterprise and research workloads.[6] Anthropic also announced a major compute partnership with **SpaceX**, securing all capacity at SpaceX’s Colossus 1 data center (over 220,000 NVIDIA GPUs and more than 300 MW of power) and using this to double code‑assistant rate limits and substantially raise API limits for Claude Opus models, signaling both strong demand and an aggressive scale‑up to train and serve more capable systems.[11] In parallel, Anthropic has publicly emphasized “recursive self‑improvement” in its research, documenting how it is already using AI systems to accelerate the development of new AI models, which could further speed innovation cycles in the field.[7]  

These moves are having visible industry impact. The expansion of Claude’s automation capabilities—such as new plug‑ins for its Claude Cowork agent that can handle complex legal, sales, marketing, and data‑analysis tasks—has contributed to investor concerns about disruption in professional services and data‑analytics firms, with some market participants explicitly citing Anthropic’s tools as a driver of sector sell‑offs.[1] At the same time, Anthropic’s growing compute footprint and deep integration with multiple cloud providers position it as one of a small handful of labs capable of training and deploying frontier‑scale models, reinforcing a trend toward concentration of AI capabilities in a few well‑capitalized actors. Its safety‑focused branding and technical work on alignment mean that its decisions on model deployment, access controls, and research directions are increasingly watched by regulators and enterprises as a bellwether for responsible AI development.[7][13]

AI Automation Society appears to be a community or membership group focused on AI and automation, hosted on Skool, rather than a major standards body or long-established industry association.[5] In the broader AI/ML and automation landscape, organizations such as A3 (Association for Advancing Automation) and ISA (International Society of Automation) are the more established institutions publishing industry news and automation-related updates, which helps frame AI Automation Society as a smaller, niche audience/community entity by comparison.[1][4][9][13]

The latest visible public signal in the search results is its Skool presence, but there were no detailed press releases, product announcements, or widely covered news items specifically about AI Automation Society in the results provided.[5] For current industry context, the most relevant adjacent sources are Reuters, WSJ, A3, ISA, and AI-focused newsletters/news hubs, which indicate that the AI/ML space remains centered on automation, enterprise adoption, and operational efficiency rather than this specific community alone.[1][2][3][4][6][7][10][12]

Skool is an online community and course platform that is being used by AI/ML-focused groups such as the **AI Automation Society** and **Skool AI Masterclass** to distribute news, discussions, and learning content around the field.[11][2][3] In that context, Skool matters less as an AI model or ML company itself and more as the *infrastructure layer* for AI communities: it helps creators bundle community, courses, and updates in one place, which is useful for fast-moving AI audiences that want ongoing curation and peer learning.[5][11]

The most recent activity visible in the provided results is a steady stream of AI-news posts hosted on Skool communities, including coverage of Nvidia’s “Space Computing” push for orbital data centers and autonomous spacecraft, along with broader AI trend roundups on models, robotics, and enterprise partnerships.[1][4][7] The industry impact is primarily distributional: Skool is helping niche AI communities rapidly organize, monetize, and retain members around timely AI/ML developments, while also serving as a channel for newsletters and training programs that translate industry news into actionable learning.[9][11]

Abhijay Arora Vuyyuru is the creator of the **AI Action Letter**, a Substack newsletter focused on practical AI, automation, and agent-based workflows for productivity, careers, and job search.[1][4] The newsletter emphasizes turning large language models into **actionable agents**—for example, using AI to build job-hunting automations, optimize resumes for ATS, and streamline professional networking, often with detailed prompts and step-by-step implementation guides.[11][12] He positions his content at the intersection of AI tools, automation platforms (like n8n and various agents), and real-world use cases for students and professionals, supported by a sizeable online audience (including a large Instagram community he references in his job-search guide).[12]

Recent developments center on hands-on AI/ML applications rather than core model research. In 2026 posts and LinkedIn updates, Abhijay highlights building **AI agents** that run 24/7 to find jobs and tailor resumes, as well as workflows that integrate LLMs with automation tools and email to fully automate outreach.[9][14][15] He has also published an updated **prompt engineering guide** for 2026 and a detailed AI guide to landing jobs or internships, framing AI as a leverage tool for upskilling, networking, and search rather than a purely technical subject.[10][12] The industry impact is primarily in **democratizing applied AI**: his work provides non-experts with concrete templates and prompts to operationalize AI in their career and productivity stacks, illustrating how agent-based systems and prompt engineering can be productized and adopted at the individual and small-team level.[2][5][8]

Ollama is an open‑source runtime and packaging layer for running large language models **locally** on laptops, workstations, and servers, with a strong focus on privacy, simple model management (via `ollama run`, pull, and custom Modelfiles), and easy integration into apps via HTTP APIs.[3][7][15] It matters because it gives developers and enterprises a practical alternative to cloud‑hosted LLM APIs, enabling on‑prem and edge deployments where data residency, latency, or cost control are critical, and it has quickly become one of the default ways to stand up local LLM backends in the AI/ML tooling ecosystem.[3][7][15]

Recent developments include the release of **Ollama v0.8**, which adds streaming responses and **tool calling** so local models can invoke external tools and real‑time web search, effectively turning a local LLM into a more agent‑like assistant.[4] Ollama has also unveiled a new **multimodal AI engine**—separate from the original llama.cpp base—implemented in Go with optimizations such as KV‑cache and image caching, chunked attention, and 2D rotary embeddings to significantly improve local reasoning performance and large‑image handling.[5] At the same time, widespread adoption has surfaced security and ops concerns: researchers have identified more than **175,000 publicly exposed Ollama servers** and critical vulnerabilities (e.g., memory‑exfiltration issues like “Bleeding Llama”) affecting hundreds of thousands of inference nodes, which has pushed security teams to treat Ollama infrastructure as high‑value, internet‑facing compute that needs proper hardening and monitoring.[1][9] Together, these advances and risks are making Ollama a central piece in local/enterprise AI stacks—powering commercial offerings (including higher‑tier usage plans layered on top of Ollama backends), influencing comparisons with frameworks like vLLM, and driving a broader industry conversation about how to safely operate self‑hosted LLM infrastructure at scale.[2][10][11][15]

missingStories.headline: GPT‑5.6 quietly rolls out to ChatGPT Pro ahead of official OpenAI launch
missingStories.summary: Multiple user reports and benchmarkers indicate that a new OpenAI model, informally labeled **GPT‑5.6**, is now powering parts of ChatGPT Pro despite no formal announcement from the company.[3] Early tests show noticeable gains in code synthesis, tool-usage reliability, and long-context reasoning compared with the previous Pro-tier model.[3]
missingStories.whyItMatters: For practitioners, this suggests OpenAI is increasingly iterating models in‑place rather than via clean versioned releases, complicating reproducibility and rigorous evaluation. Teams building on ChatGPT’s Pro tier need to be aware that behavior, latency, and capabilities may change without explicit version bumps, making explicit evaluation harnesses and regression tests around prompts even more important.
missingStories.source: unrot.co AI News Today June 21 2026 report on GPT‑5.6 behavior changes in ChatGPT Pro

missingStories.headline: New 'Agentjacking' attack exposes AI coding agents via Sentry error‑tracking integration
missingStories.summary: Security researchers disclosed a new attack class dubbed **Agentjacking**, which targets AI coding agents integrated with the Sentry error‑tracking platform.[3] By poisoning error payloads and stack traces, attackers were able to trick agents into running malicious code locally, achieving an 85% exploitation rate across 2,388 organizations in tests.[3]
missingStories.whyItMatters: As more teams wire autonomous or semi‑autonomous agents into their dev and ops stacks, this shows that observability and logging tools can become high‑impact prompt‑injection and code‑execution vectors. Practitioners need to treat all external telemetry, bug reports, and traces as untrusted input in agent loops, and build explicit sandboxing, allow‑lists, and security review layers around AI‑driven code actions.
missingStories.source: unrot.co AI News Today June 21 2026 coverage of the Agentjacking vulnerability research

missingStories.headline: ChatGPT falls below 50% global AI assistant market share for the first time
missingStories.summary: Sensor Tower’s 2026 State of AI Report shows ChatGPT’s share of the global AI assistant market dropped to **46.4%** by late May 2026, marking the first time it has held less than half of the market since launch.[3] Competing assistants from Google, Meta, Anthropic, and open‑source frontends collectively gained share over the past year.[3]
missingStories.whyItMatters: This shift signals a structurally more competitive assistant and agent ecosystem, weakening any single‑vendor default. For builders, it increases the importance of multi‑model backends, portability across providers, and UX layers that can swap models without rewriting entire products.
missingStories.source: unrot.co summary of Sensor Tower 2026 State of AI market‑share data

missingStories.headline: Free access window for Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 ends as paid pricing kicks in
missingStories.summary: Anthropic is ending the free promotional window for its flagship Fable 5 model, moving to a pricing structure of around **$10 per million input tokens** and **$50 per million output tokens** for ongoing access starting June 23.[5] This shift comes amid ongoing export‑control‑driven suspensions of Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for many users, adding commercial and policy pressure to the models’ rollout.[1][5]
missingStories.whyItMatters: The end of free access sets a clearer reference price for top‑tier frontier models and affects cost projections for teams that piloted on the promo window. Practitioners need to revisit ROI calculations, consider model‑mixing (cheaper + frontier), and plan for potential regional or nationality‑based access constraints when deploying products on Anthropic’s stack.
missingStories.source: BuildFastWithAI June 21 2026 and PromptAI Learning weekly roundup on Fable 5 pricing changes

missingStories.headline: Google prepares to ship Chrome auto‑browse agent baked into Android at massive scale
missingStories.summary: Google is days away from shipping a **Chrome auto‑browse agent** integrated directly into the Android operating system, putting autonomous browsing and action capabilities on hundreds of millions of devices.[2] This follows a commitment from Sundar Pichai that major Gemini 3.5 upgrades, including deeper agentic behavior, would land by late June.[2]
missingStories.whyItMatters: OS‑level agents that can navigate the web and act on behalf of users represent a step change from chatbots confined to a tab. For practitioners, this opens new surfaces for automation products, but also raises safety, abuse, and SEO/search‑disruption questions; designing agent‑friendly sites, APIs, and guardrails around autonomous web actions will become more urgent.
missingStories.source: PromptAI Learning Daily AI News June 21 2026 coverage of Chrome auto‑browse agent and Gemini 3.5 timing
